items.question:
A grant officer asks Claude to extract all award conditions from a 50-page federal grant agreement. The extraction misses six conditions embedded in complex conditional structures: "If the grantee fails to... the award may be..." The officer asks what is causing the omissions.

What is the MOST likely cause?

options.A: The prompt provided no examples showing how to extract conditions from conditional sentence structures, so Claude did not apply that pattern to the if-then constructions.
options.B: Federal grant language uses specialised vocabulary that Claude cannot parse without domain-specific training.
options.C: Fifty pages exceeds the practical document length for extraction tasks.
options.D: The prompt asked for "conditions" but the correct legal term is "obligations" — the terminology mismatch caused the misses.

items.question:
A product analyst sends Claude a 600-word prompt containing: company background, target market context, six feature ideas, competitive landscape notes, three operational constraints, and a final question asking for a priority ranking of the features. The response ranks only two of the six features and ignores the constraints entirely.

What is the PRIMARY structural flaw in this prompt?

options.A: Six features exceed the number Claude can rank in a single prompt.
options.B: The prompt mixes background context, analytical content, and task instructions without structural separation, making it difficult for Claude to identify what it is being asked to do.
options.C: The prompt should have been submitted via API rather than the chat interface.
options.D: Six hundred words exceeds the practical character limit for a single message.

items.question:
A policy researcher uploads a 200-page government regulation and asks: "What is the penalty for a first-time violation of Section 14(b)?" The response describes the general penalty framework but does not cite Section 14(b) specifically.

What is the MOST effective prompt adjustment?

options.A: Ask Claude to summarise the entire regulation before answering the specific question.
options.B: Upload the regulation in sections rather than as one large file.
options.C: Direct Claude to search specifically within Section 14(b), quote the relevant text, and then answer the question — rather than asking a general question about the full document.
options.D: Switch to Research mode to allow Claude to cross-reference external regulatory databases.

items.question:
A financial analyst uses a three-stage prompt chain across three separate days. On day three she starts a new chat session for Stage 3. The Stage 3 output references "the previous analysis" but the content is generic — the specific findings from days one and two do not appear.

What is the MOST likely cause?

options.A: Claude cannot access files shared in previous sessions through the standard chat interface.
options.B: Starting a new session on day three reset the model's conversation memory from days one and two.
options.C: A three-day prompt chain exceeds the maximum session duration for chained workflows.
options.D: The Stage 1 and Stage 2 outputs were not embedded in the Stage 3 prompt — Claude had no access to the upstream findings.

items.question:
A senior manager uploads three policy documents and a compliance checklist in a single long prompt. Claude's response addresses some checklist items but misses others, and references only policy document one while ignoring documents two and three. (Choose TWO)

Which TWO structural fixes are MOST likely to improve coverage across all three documents?

options.A: Wrap each document in descriptively named XML tags — `<policy_1>`, `<policy_2>`, `<policy_3>` — to delineate their content boundaries.
options.B: Merge the three policy documents into a single combined document before uploading to reduce prompt complexity.
options.C: Instruct Claude to address each checklist item one by one, citing the relevant policy document for each finding.
options.D: Reorder the three documents so the most relevant one appears last in the prompt.
options.E: Ask Claude to confirm it has read all three policy documents before beginning the compliance review.

items.question:
A technical consultant pastes a product specification document directly into a prompt followed by analysis instructions, with no separator between them. Claude's response edits sections of the specification rather than producing an analysis.

What is the MOST direct cause?

options.A: Without structural delimiters, Claude cannot reliably distinguish content to analyse from instructions to follow — the specification and instructions merge into an undifferentiated text block.
options.B: Product specification documents use a technical format that Claude cannot parse without a structured import mode.
options.C: Analysis tasks require a separate prompt from the document submission; they cannot be combined in one message.
options.D: The instructions should have been placed before the document for Claude to treat them as directives.

items.question:
An analyst builds a few-shot prompt to detect financial reporting anomalies. The three examples all show high-severity, obvious anomalies. In production, the prompt misses subtle anomalies — small rounding discrepancies and unusual intercompany allocations — that auditors consider material.

What is the MOST precise diagnosis?

options.A: Three examples are too few for anomaly detection; a minimum of ten is recommended.
options.B: Obvious and subtle anomalies require different models because they require different levels of reasoning depth.
options.C: The examples did not include subtle or boundary-case anomalies, so Claude has no signal for what those patterns look like in this financial context.
options.D: Subtle anomalies cannot be detected through prompting and require custom fine-tuning on proprietary financial data.

items.question:
A data team builds a four-stage prompt chain to generate patient cohort criteria: Stage 1 (inclusion criteria from guidelines), Stage 2 (structured query logic), Stage 3 (clinical validation), Stage 4 (patient consent language). All stages run automatically with no human review. Stage 2 introduces a logical negation error. Stage 3 validation runs against Stage 2's flawed output. Stage 4 consent language is generated from Stage 3's compromised validation.

What is the MOST significant design flaw?

options.A: The chain was too long; four stages should be collapsed to two for a clinical workflow.
options.B: Clinical logic translation should always use a specialised model trained on healthcare data.
options.C: Stage 3 was designed as a validation step but was executed by Claude without a human clinician reviewing the output, making it ineffective as a quality gate.
options.D: The automated pipeline removed human review checkpoints between stages, allowing a Stage 2 error to propagate silently through Stages 3 and 4 into patient-facing consent documentation.

items.question:
A regulatory affairs manager asks Claude to evaluate whether a product modification triggers re-registration requirements. She adds "think step by step" to make the reasoning visible. Claude produces a detailed four-step analysis concluding no re-registration is required. She submits without expert review. A regulatory consultant later finds that Step 3 applied the wrong product-category threshold.

What lesson does this scenario MOST directly illustrate?

options.A: Chain-of-thought should not be used for regulatory tasks because it produces complex output that is difficult to review.
options.B: The detailed reasoning output confirms the analysis was thorough before submission.
options.C: Claude should have been instructed to express uncertainty explicitly if it was unsure of any step.
options.D: Visible reasoning is auditable but not self-certifying — detailed steps can contain errors, and expert review remains required for high-stakes regulatory determinations.

items.question:
A supply chain analyst is debugging a three-stage prompt chain that produces a generic remediation plan in Stage 3. She has confirmed: Stage 1 correctly identified six supplier risk flags; Stage 2 produced a risk prioritisation matrix. She is now diagnosing why Stage 3 is generic.

What should she check FIRST?

options.A: Whether the Stage 3 prompt specifies the correct model tier for remediation planning.
options.B: Whether the Stage 1 and Stage 2 outputs are explicitly included in the Stage 3 prompt.
options.C: Whether the Stage 3 prompt is too short to produce a detailed remediation plan.
options.D: Whether the supplier risk categories in Stage 1 fall within Claude's domain knowledge.

items.question:
A management consultant builds a prompt to analyse a client's 80-page strategic plan. The 800-word prompt contains the document, nine specific analysis questions, three formatting requirements, a persona instruction, a word limit, and a style guide reference. The output addresses four of the nine questions and ignores the style guide entirely. (Choose TWO)

Which TWO factors MOST likely caused these failures?

options.A: The persona instruction overrides all other formatting requirements when included in the same prompt.
options.B: The model tier used was insufficient for an 80-page document.
options.C: Nine simultaneous analysis questions exceed what a single prompt can reliably address — some questions are deprioritised.
options.D: The prompt contained too many competing instructions, causing Claude to selectively execute the most prominent ones and treat peripheral constraints like the style guide as optional.
options.E: Style guide instructions must be provided as examples rather than cited by name to take effect.

items.question:
A content manager at a non-profit wants Claude to produce quality assessments of incoming grant proposals. She has two hand-written assessments from her team that represent the desired format. She is setting up the prompt for the first time.

What combination of prompt elements is MOST likely to produce consistently well-structured assessments?

options.A: Place the grant proposal first, then the two hand-written assessments as examples, followed by the task instruction.
options.B: Place the task instruction first, then the two examples, then the grant proposal.
options.C: Submit the grant proposal in one message and the examples in a separate follow-up message.
options.D: Use chain-of-thought prompting to replace the need for examples in quality assessment tasks.

items.question:
A bid manager uses a few-shot prompt to evaluate RFP responses. He embeds three example evaluations in the same prompt as the real RFP text. Claude sometimes incorporates language from the examples as if it were part of the actual RFP being evaluated.

What is the SIMPLEST fix?

options.A: Remove the examples and rely on precise prose instructions to describe the evaluation format.
options.B: Wrap each example in `<example>...</example>` tags and the real RFP in `<rfp>...</rfp>` tags to clearly separate demonstration content from content to evaluate.
options.C: Submit examples in a separate conversation before the RFP evaluation prompt.
options.D: Reduce the examples to one to minimise the mixing risk.

items.question:
A strategy analyst at a private equity firm needs an investment thesis covering market sizing, competitive positioning, and risk assessment for a board meeting. She is deciding between (a) a single prompt with chain-of-thought covering all three analyses, or (b) three separate prompts with human review between each.

What is the MOST appropriate design?

options.A: Use a single prompt with chain-of-thought — the three analyses can be sequenced effectively within one well-structured prompt.
options.B: Use three separate prompts but skip intermediate review for workflow speed.
options.C: Decompose into three separate prompts with human review between each, and use CoT within each stage so the reasoning is auditable at every step.
options.D: Use chain-of-thought in Stage 1 only; once market sizing is established, subsequent stages do not benefit from visible reasoning.

items.question:
A compliance officer uploads a 60-page regulatory framework to Claude and asks: "What does this say?" The response is a general three-paragraph overview of the document's structure. The officer needed information about a specific section on reporting timelines.

What is the PRIMARY reason for this vague output?

options.A: Sixty pages exceeds the practical document length for Claude's precise analysis.
options.B: The compliance officer should have used Research mode for regulatory document questions.
options.C: The document was uploaded before the question was specified, causing a processing order issue.
options.D: The question was too general — without a specific topic or section focus, Claude defaulted to a broad overview.

items.question: An internal audit manager at a global bank needs a reliable workflow where Claude classifies 200 vendor contracts by risk tier and then drafts a risk summary report for the Audit Committee. She asks which design decisions are MOST important. (Choose TWO)

options.A: Use the highest-tier model to ensure accurate classification across all 200 contracts.
options.B: Add representative few-shot examples for each risk tier before deploying classification at volume.
options.C: Run classification and summary drafting in a single prompt for workflow efficiency.
options.D: Decompose classification from summary drafting, with human review of classifications before the summary is generated.
options.E: Submit all 200 contract texts in a single prompt to ensure consistent classification logic.

items.question:
A policy analyst builds a prompt containing a 40-page policy document, a 12-item review criteria list, and a task instruction to evaluate the policy against the criteria. She uses no structural markers. Claude's evaluation mixes criteria language into the policy analysis rather than treating criteria as the evaluation framework.

What is the SIMPLEST structural improvement?

options.A: Use XML tags to separate the policy document, review criteria, and task instructions into distinct, labelled sections.
options.B: Submit the review criteria in a separate message before the policy document.
options.C: Add chain-of-thought prompting to require Claude to address each criterion explicitly.
options.D: Reduce the policy document to the sections most relevant to the criteria before submitting.

items.question:
A research analyst at an asset management firm builds a two-stage chain: Stage 1 generates a structured earnings analysis from a company transcript; Stage 2 drafts an investment note from the Stage 1 analysis. She has example investment notes from her firm that show the required format and tone.

In which stage should the examples be placed, and why?

options.A: Stage 1, so Claude understands the final output goal before drafting the interim analysis.
options.B: Stage 2, where the target format is the investment note — the stage that directly produces the output the examples demonstrate.
options.C: Both stages, so the format expectation is consistent throughout the chain.
options.D: Neither stage — once the chain is structured, structural examples add unnecessary prompt length.

items.question:
An M&A analyst needs Claude to review a 100-page target company prospectus, identify all disclosed litigation risks, and rank them by potential financial impact. Initial attempts using a general extraction request miss risks in appendices.

What is the MOST effective prompt structure?

options.A: Place task instructions first, then the document, then add "think step by step" for the ranking.
options.B: Ask Claude to summarise the prospectus first, then extract litigation risks from the summary, then rank by impact.
options.C: Place the prospectus first in the prompt, then instruct Claude to identify litigation risks section by section before ranking by financial impact.
options.D: Decompose into three separate prompts: one for identification across the full document, one for extraction, and one for ranking.

items.question:
A knowledge manager is classifying 500 client engagement documents into seven practice areas. Two examples per practice area (14 examples total) produce accurate classification for five areas but struggle with two that have overlapping vocabulary. She considers (a) adding more examples for the two difficult areas, or (b) decomposing into two prompts — a general classifier and a second specifically tuned for the difficult areas.

What is the MOST appropriate first step?

options.A: Add more examples across all seven areas proportionally before addressing the two specific areas.
options.B: Decompose immediately — adding examples is not effective for vocabulary-overlap classification problems.
options.C: Switch to a higher-tier model for the two difficult areas and keep the existing prompt for the other five.
options.D: Add targeted examples for the two difficult areas first to determine whether the accuracy gap closes before committing to the complexity of decomposition.

items.question:
A financial controller uses a three-stage prompt chain: Stage 1 produces a revenue forecast; Stage 2 reconciles the forecast against actuals; Stage 3 writes CFO commentary. She is adding chain-of-thought prompting to one stage and asks which stage benefits most.

Which stage benefits MOST from chain-of-thought, and why?

options.A: Stage 2 — reconciliation requires identifying variances and tracing their causes, steps the CFO needs to verify explicitly.
options.B: Stage 3 — the written commentary needs to explain its logic clearly to be useful to the CFO.
options.C: Stage 1 — revenue forecasting is the most complex analytical task and benefits most from visible reasoning.
options.D: All three stages equally — chain-of-thought is always appropriate in a multi-stage financial pipeline.

items.question:
A clinical trial manager at a biotech firm is building a prompt to classify protocol deviations as Major, Minor, or Procedural. Classification errors in this context can affect patient safety and regulatory submissions. She is deciding between prose instructions and few-shot examples.

What is the MOST important consideration for this decision?

options.A: Major, Minor, and Procedural are standard clinical terms that Claude classifies correctly from instructions alone.
options.B: For high-stakes classification where errors carry patient safety and regulatory consequences, concrete examples that anchor each class are a lower-risk approach than prose instructions that may be ambiguously interpreted.
options.C: The choice depends primarily on the length of the deviation reports rather than on the stakes involved.
options.D: Regulatory contexts always require the highest-tier model regardless of whether examples are used.

items.question:
A senior auditor evaluates vendor security assessments. Each assessment is 20 pages long. She needs Claude to evaluate each against 15 control criteria and flag gaps. Initial attempts return incomplete coverage — some criteria are never addressed.

What prompt structure MOST reliably ensures all 15 criteria are covered?

options.A: Add chain-of-thought and ask Claude to evaluate all 15 criteria together before summarising.
options.B: Provide example evaluations that show all 15 criteria addressed in completed assessments.
options.C: Wrap the assessment in `<assessment>...</assessment>` tags and the 15 criteria in `<criteria>...</criteria>` tags, then instruct Claude to address each criterion in turn.
options.D: Submit the assessment and the 15 criteria in separate messages sequentially.

items.question:
An attorney uploads a 180-page merger agreement and asks Claude to "review this contract." The response is a superficial three-paragraph summary. The attorney reports the output is inadequate and asks for a diagnosis.

What is the CORRECT diagnosis?

options.A: One hundred eighty pages exceeds Claude's document processing limit for detailed analysis.
options.B: Contract review requires domain-specific legal training that Claude does not have.
options.C: Claude should have used Research mode to supplement the contract with external legal databases.
options.D: The prompt lacked a defined review scope — without specific questions or criteria, Claude defaulted to a high-level overview rather than a targeted analysis.

items.question:
A grants officer at a foundation reviews 30 grant applications per cycle. Applications vary significantly in writing quality and completeness. She wants to build a reliable Claude-assisted review workflow. (Choose TWO)

Which TWO design decisions are MOST important?

options.A: Use few-shot examples from previous funded and declined applications to anchor scoring tier definitions concretely.
options.B: Submit all 30 applications in a single batch prompt to ensure scoring consistency across applications.
options.C: Decompose into a scoring stage and a recommendation memo stage, with grants officer review of all scores before memos are drafted.
options.D: Use the highest-tier model to handle variation in application writing quality.
options.E: Allow Claude to produce final funding decisions without human review to reduce cycle time.

items.question:
A regulatory analyst at a pharmaceutical company needs Claude to extract all post-market surveillance obligations from a 120-page regulatory guidance document. A general extraction prompt missed obligations in subsection footnotes.

What combination of strategies is MOST effective?

options.A: Place the guidance document first in the prompt, then instruct Claude to scan each section in sequence and list obligations found per section before compiling a final list.
options.B: Ask Claude to summarise the document and then extract obligations from the summary.
options.C: Enable Research mode to supplement the guidance document with external regulatory databases.
options.D: Break the document into 10-page chunks and submit each as a separate prompt.

items.question:
A legal operations manager must review a 250-page enterprise software contract for 20 risk categories. She considers (a) submitting the full contract with all 20 categories in a single prompt, or (b) running 20 separate prompts, one per risk category. A colleague argues one approach is always better.

What is the MOST nuanced and accurate assessment?

options.A: Approach (a) is always better because all risks are evaluated in a unified contextual view of the contract.
options.B: Approach (b) is always better because single-category focus guarantees more thorough analysis per category.
options.C: Approach (a) is more appropriate for categories that are broadly distributed and require cross-contract contextual awareness; approach (b) is more appropriate for categories requiring targeted depth in a specific contract area.
options.D: Approach (b) is always better because submitting 20 categories in one prompt exceeds recommended prompt scope.

items.question:
A procurement head uses a three-stage chain with chain-of-thought in each stage: Stage 1 scores a supplier on criteria with visible reasoning; Stage 2 identifies commercial risks with visible reasoning; Stage 3 produces a recommendation with visible reasoning. Company policy requires human sign-off before any decision.

At which stages should human review occur, and what is the PRIMARY purpose of CoT in this workflow?

options.A: Human review at Stage 3 only; CoT accelerates Stage 1 and Stage 2 processing.
options.B: Human review at Stage 1 only; CoT in later stages reduces the need for review of downstream outputs.
options.C: No human review is needed because CoT makes all reasoning transparent and self-certifying.
options.D: Human review at each stage gate; CoT makes each stage's reasoning auditable so the reviewer can evaluate the logic, not just the conclusion, at every step.

items.question:
A chief compliance officer at a global bank wants Claude to assist with regulatory examination findings. Each finding requires: classification by severity, root cause identification, and a formal management response. Initial tests produce generic responses that do not reference the specific examination language. (Choose TWO)

Which TWO design changes MOST directly address the generic output?

options.A: Include two previous examination findings and their approved management responses as examples, anchoring the expected format and level of specificity.
options.B: Switch to the highest-tier model for all three subtasks.
options.C: Decompose into three separate prompts — classification, root cause, and response drafting — and embed the specific examination finding text in each stage's prompt.
options.D: Apply chain-of-thought to the response drafting stage only, since the response is the client-facing output.
options.E: Use XML tags to separate classification results from root cause analysis in the final output.

items.question:
A management consultant has a two-stage prompt chain analysing a client's operating model. Stage 1 produces a reasonable structural analysis but lacks specificity. Stage 2 produces generic recommendations that do not reference Stage 1 findings. She is deciding whether to fix Stage 1 first or Stage 2 first.

What should she do FIRST?

options.A: Fix Stage 1 to improve its specificity — better input will naturally improve Stage 2 output.
options.B: Fix the Stage 2 state handoff first — confirm the Stage 1 output is explicitly embedded in Stage 2 before investing in Stage 1 improvements.
options.C: Add chain-of-thought to both stages so the reasoning is visible before making any changes.
options.D: Switch to a higher-tier model for Stage 2 to compensate for specificity gaps.

items.question:
A senior vice president at an insurance company is designing a Claude-assisted underwriting workflow for complex commercial risks. The workflow must be reliable (consistent decisions), auditable (explainable to regulators), and safe (no unreviewed recommendations reach underwriters). (Choose TWO)

Which TWO design principles MOST directly satisfy all three requirements?

options.A: Use a single comprehensive prompt to ensure all underwriting factors are considered in a unified context.
options.B: Use task decomposition with an underwriter reviewing and approving each stage output before it becomes input to the next stage.
options.C: Use few-shot examples only for simple risk categories; rely on instructions alone for complex ones.
options.D: Apply chain-of-thought within each stage so the reasoning behind each analytical step is visible for underwriter review and regulator explanation.
options.E: Use the highest-tier model to eliminate the need for intermediate review steps.

items.question:
A policy analyst at a government agency writes a 200-word prompt with three paragraphs of bill background, a paragraph on stakeholder concerns, then ends with: "Oh, and could you draft a two-paragraph plain-English summary suitable for a press release?" Claude produces a thorough policy analysis but does not generate the press release summary.

What is the PRIMARY cause?

options.A: Claude truncated the prompt before reaching the final sentence due to an input length limit.
options.B: Press release language conflicts with Claude's default mode for policy analysis prompts.
options.C: The background context established a detailed-analysis frame; the final instruction was treated as supplementary commentary rather than the primary task.
options.D: The core task was buried at the end of extensive preamble, causing Claude to optimise for what the majority of the prompt framed rather than the final sentence.

items.question:
A learning and development manager asks Claude to "generate a quiz about cybersecurity basics." Claude returns 15 questions of varying difficulty. The manager needed exactly 10 questions at consistent medium difficulty for a 20-minute module.

Which prompt change would MOST precisely produce the intended output?

options.A: "Generate exactly 10 multiple-choice questions about cybersecurity basics. Each question should be medium difficulty — requires applying a concept, not just recalling a definition. Include four options per question and mark the correct answer."
options.B: "Generate a shorter cybersecurity quiz with fewer questions."
options.C: "Generate a cybersecurity quiz suitable for a 20-minute training module."
options.D: "Generate 10 cybersecurity questions."

items.question:
An operations analyst sends Claude: "Could you possibly, if it's not too much trouble, perhaps help me by kindly reviewing this process document and letting me know what you think might potentially be improved in terms of clarity?" Claude returns a vague response noting the document "appears generally clear with some potential areas that might benefit from attention."

What is the MOST direct fix?

options.A: Add a role instruction: "You are an expert process documentation reviewer."
options.B: Replace the hedged prompt with a direct instruction: "Review this process document. Identify specific unclear steps, ambiguous terms, and missing decision points. List each issue with a suggested fix."
options.C: Append "Please be blunt in your feedback" to the existing prompt.
options.D: Upload the document to a Project knowledge base before requesting the review.

items.question:
A management consultant needs a competitive analysis of three firms across five strategic dimensions for a client presentation. He prompts: "Give me a brief analysis." Claude returns five single sentences — one per dimension, averaged across all three firms with no firm-level differentiation.

What is the BEST correction?

options.A: Replace "brief" with "comprehensive" to signal that greater depth is expected.
options.B: Ask Claude to redo the analysis "with more detail on each firm."
options.C: Replace "Give me a brief analysis" with explicit scope: "For each of the three firms, analyse these five dimensions: [list]. Write 2–3 sentences of firm-specific observations per dimension. Total: approximately 450 words."
options.D: Split the task into three separate prompts, one per firm, and manually consolidate the results.

items.question: A data analyst at a 90,000-employee insurance firm asks Claude to process 50 claim records and produce a summary report. The report must serve two purposes: import into a BI tool and sharing with senior executives. Which TWO format specifications should be included in the prompt to serve both audiences? (Choose TWO)

options.A: "Write the full summary in narrative paragraph form."
options.B: "Output each claim record as a structured JSON or CSV row for system import."
options.C: "Use the Opus model for better output formatting quality."
options.D: "Include an executive summary section with 3–5 bullet points highlighting key trends."
options.E: "Limit the entire response to 200 words for executive readability."

items.question: A UX writer at a 12-person healthtech startup is refining onboarding tooltip messages with Claude in a single conversation. Which TWO situations should trigger starting a NEW iterative refinement loop rather than continuing in the current conversation? (Choose TWO)

options.A: The conversation has drifted so far from the original brief that Claude is now optimising against a different success criterion than the one the writer started with.
options.B: Claude returned a response that was 15 words longer than the specified limit.
options.C: The writer decides to change the target user persona from 'power user' to 'first-time user,' fundamentally reframing the task.
options.D: One of the twelve tooltips contains a passive construction that Claude missed.
options.E: Claude asked a clarifying question about which screen the tooltip appears on.

items.question:
A financial analyst at a mid-market investment firm is producing a sector comparison memo with Claude. Her first run returned the correct five-section structure but only one-sentence summaries per sector — far shallower than the 3–4 sentence analytical paragraphs she needs. She has confirmed the structure is correct and wants to fix only the depth.

What should she do NEXT?

options.A: Switch to Opus for stronger reasoning on financial content.
options.B: Start a new conversation with the original prompt to see if depth varies across runs.
options.C: Add all sector context documents to a Project knowledge base before re-running.
options.D: Add a targeted depth instruction to the existing prompt: specify the required paragraph length and provide a brief example of the expected analytical depth for the first sector.

items.question: A senior consultant is reviewing a colleague's prompt before adding it to the team template library. The prompt instructs Claude to: "summarise AND provide full detail, be concise AND comprehensive, and write for experts AND explain all terminology." Which TWO anti-patterns does this prompt demonstrate? (Choose TWO)

options.A: Politeness padding that reduces instruction directness.
options.B: Conflicting instructions that give Claude two mutually exclusive success criteria simultaneously.
options.C: A buried ask hidden beneath excessive background context.
options.D: Kitchen-sink framing that stacks incompatible output requirements into a single prompt.
options.E: Over-specification that unnecessarily constrains Claude's output.

items.question: A legal operations team at a global enterprise is building a prompt template library for contract review tasks. Which TWO benefits does a well-structured prompt template provide compared to ad hoc prompts written by individual team members? (Choose TWO)

options.A: Consistent output structure across all team members running the same task, regardless of individual prompting style.
options.B: Elimination of the need for human review because the template enforces quality.
options.C: A repeatable starting point that captures the firm's specific risk categories, terminology, and output format requirements.
options.D: Automatic integration with the firm's contract management system.
options.E: Guaranteed identical output on every run due to template precision.

items.question: What is the primary contractual distinction between a consumer AI tool and an enterprise AI agreement regarding submitted data?

options.A: Enterprise tools always use more powerful model tiers, resulting in higher-quality outputs.
options.B: Consumer tools are limited to personal use only; enterprise tools are limited to business use only.
options.C: Enterprise agreements include dedicated server infrastructure that is not shared with other customers.
options.D: Enterprise agreements typically prohibit the provider from training on submitted data; consumer terms often permit such use.

items.question: Which TWO controls reduce the risk of prompt injection from documents processed by an AI tool? (Choose TWO)

options.A: Applying structural boundaries in the prompt that clearly separate the AI's instructions from the document content
options.B: Increasing output temperature so the model is more likely to follow only the most recent instruction it encounters
options.C: Reviewing AI outputs for unexpected instructions or behaviours before taking any downstream action
options.D: Compressing documents before uploading to prevent hidden characters from reaching the model
options.E: Using a higher-tier model because more capable models are inherently resistant to injection

items.question: What IP risk arises when an AI model generates text that closely resembles copyrighted material in its training data?

options.A: The organisation must pay a royalty to the model developer for each commercial use of the output.
options.B: The AI output may reproduce protected expression from training data, potentially infringing the original copyright holder's rights when used commercially.
options.C: The AI vendor is automatically and exclusively liable for any copyright infringement in outputs because it designed the training process.
options.D: The organisation acquires an implied licence to use the material because the AI processed it as part of a lawful commercial service.

items.question: When AI output has caused harm to a data subject, what is the organisation's FIRST governance priority before investigating root cause?

options.A: Contain further harm by stopping or correcting the erroneous output and preserving evidence for investigation.
options.B: Notify the AI vendor immediately so they can issue a model patch.
options.C: Publish a transparency report disclosing the incident publicly within 24 hours.
options.D: Suspend all AI tools organisation-wide until the root cause is confirmed and remediated.

items.question: Why does shadow AI specifically complicate data breach discovery and regulatory notification for an organisation?

options.A: Shadow AI tools use stronger encryption than approved tools, making breach signals technically harder to detect.
options.B: Regulators exempt incidents involving shadow AI from breach notification requirements because the tool was unauthorised.
options.C: Unapproved tools route data through anonymous proxy servers that mask breach indicators from monitoring systems.
options.D: The organisation has no visibility into the unapproved tool's infrastructure, so it may not learn of a breach in that environment until after the notification deadline has passed.

items.question: What must an organisation establish before granting a team an exception to its AI acceptable-use policy?

options.A: Written consent from every employee in the team confirming they understand the exception applies to them.
options.B: A vendor-issued security certificate confirming the tool meets enterprise security standards.
options.C: A documented risk assessment, defined boundaries for the exception, and a review date to reassess the need.
options.D: Board-level sign-off from at least two executive directors before any exception takes effect.

items.question: What transparency obligation may arise when externally distributing content substantially written by an AI model?

options.A: Recipients or affected parties may be entitled to know that AI contributed materially to the content, particularly in regulated or high-stakes communications.
options.B: No disclosure obligation exists because AI-generated text is indistinguishable from human-written text.
options.C: The AI vendor must be named as a co-author on any externally distributed AI-generated document.
